sec.title: Purpose
sec.p: To investigate whether SIRT4 protects the optic nerve by regulating mitochondrial function and lipid metabolism in neurotoxic reactive astrocytes in the retinal ischemia-reperfusion injury.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Using SIRT4 knockout, wild-type, and overexpressing mouse ischemia-reperfusion (I/R) models, we assessed retinal ganglion cell loss, protein expression (SIRT4, APOL6, GBP2, mitochondrial dynamics), and conducted metabolomic/transcriptomic analyses. In vitro, primary astrocytes were treated with TIC cytokines; SIRT4 was knocked down via lentivirus, followed by measurement of ATP, lipid secretion, and mitochondrial morphology/function.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: SIRT4 was highly expressed in astrocytes. Its knockdown exacerbated I/R injury, promoting a neurotoxic astrocyte phenotype with increased APOL6 expression, and elevated secretion of long-chain fatty acids and phosphatidylcholines and mitochondrial damage. SIRT4 deficiency enhanced astrocyte susceptibility to injury, further reducing ATP production and worsening lipid accumulation and optic nerve damage.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: SIRT4 plays a protective role in retinal ischemia-reperfusion injury model by regulating astrocyte lipid metabolism and mitochondrial function, offering a potential therapeutic target for neuroprotection.
Keywords: retinal ischemia-reperfusion injury, SIRT4, neurodegeneration, neurotoxic reactive astrocytes, lipid metabolism, apolipoprotein, mitochondria

body.p: Retinal neurodegenerative changes occur in a variety of ophthalmic diseases, such as diabetic retinopathy, age-related macular degeneration, and optic nerve-related disorders, particularly in glaucoma.1,2 The main feature is the progressive degeneration of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), which impacts the optic nerve, lateral geniculate body, and visual cortex, ultimately leading to irreversible blindness.1,2 The ischemia-reperfusion (I/R) can lead to a disruption of retinal blood supply similar to that caused by diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma or retinal artery occlusion, resulting in damage or loss of RGCs, thinning and loss of the nerve fiber layer, and ultimately severe visual impairment or even irreversible vision loss.1 Current clinical intervention measures still struggle to effectively halt the progressive degeneration of RGCs and the optic nerve. This makes it imperative to dissect the core mechanisms underlying their degenerative changes and to identify new targets for the protection of RGCs and the optic nerve, which are key areas that urgently need breakthroughs in the field of ophthalmology.

Astrocytes serve multiple roles in helping to maintain homeostatic physiology of central nervous system tissue, astrocytes are especially critical in axonal tracts such as the optic nerve, where axons propagate energy-demanding action potentials great distances.2 In disease, astrocytes can rapidly form “reactive astrocytes” in response to any abnormal conditions. Astrocytes were classified into two types: harmful (neurotoxic/A1) or beneficial (neuroprotective/A2).3 This classification has certain limitations as it may overlook the complexity and heterogeneity of astrocytes after activation. However, the A1 and A2 classification criteria provide clear detection indicators for researchers. This study still adopts a simple dichotomy method.4 Under glaucomatous pathological conditions, astrocytes release neurotoxic factors, including cytokines and chemokines, which contribute to the degeneration of RGC axons.5–7 Furthermore, elevated lipid content in reactive astrocytes has been identified as a primary contributor to their neurotoxic phenotype.8 Previous studies have shown that inhibiting the formation of reactive astrocytes can effectively prevent neuronal loss in both acute optic nerve compression and chronic glaucoma models, thereby preserving the electrophysiological functionality of surviving neurons.7 Optic nerve head (ONH) astrocytes have been implicated in the pathogenesis of various optic neuropathies, including glaucoma and traumatic injuries.9,10 Focusing on distinct astrocyte populations, such as retinal versus optic nerve astrocytes, may yield greater therapeutic benefits in different disease contexts, particularly in glaucoma, where ONH astrocytes have been more directly implicated.11

Studies have shown that RGCs and astrocytes can transfer mitochondria to each other.12 When astrocyte mitochondria become dysfunctional, their ability to provide neuroprotection to RGCs is substantially diminished and may even exert detrimental effects on these neurons.13 SIRT4, as a member of the NAD+-dependent deacetylase Sirtuins family, is mainly located in mitochondria14 and exhibits ADP-ribosyltransferase, lipoylase, and deacylase activities.15 SIRT4 is highly expressed in glial cells of the postnatal brain, especially in astrocytes and radial glial cells during embryogenesis. SIRT4 may regulate the glutamate-glutamine cycle in the retina through multiple pathways.16 Neurotoxic reactive astrocytes can transport long-chain fatty acids (LCFA) and phosphatidylcholine (PC) to the axons of RGCs via APOE and APOJ. The accumulation of these lipids in axons exerts toxic effects, ultimately leading to fatty acid-mediated apoptosis.17 The specific mechanism by which astrocytes release LCFA and PC is currently unclear. Additionally, SIRT4 has been found to be highly expressed in astrocyte mitochondria and coordinates the balance between lipid synthesis and catabolism by inhibiting the activity of malonyl-CoA decarboxylase.18

Our previous research explored the localization and function of Sirtuins in the retina,19 demonstrating that SIRT4 protects Müller glial cells by regulating mitochondrial dynamics and oxidative stress.20 Furthermore, SIRT4 promotes OPA1-mediated mitochondrial fusion in Müller glial cells and GLAST expression, thereby protecting the retina from glaucomatous excitotoxic damage.21 However, the precise mechanism underlying SIRT4 function in astrocytes remains to be fully elucidated. Therefore, we aimed to integrate the in vivo model (I/R model) with the in vitro model (neurotoxic reactive astrocyte TIC model) to comprehensively investigate the specific role and mechanism of SIRT4 in the process of optic nerve injury. This research will provide an effective and feasible direction for optic nerve protection, and may reveal potential therapeutic targets.

sec.title: Animals
sec.p: Male wild-type C57BL/6 mice and SIRT4-knockout (KO) mice were used in this study, and 6–8-weeks-old mice were purchased from Beijing Sibeifu Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (license number: SCXK [Jing] 2019–0010). Animal treatment and care were approved by the Animal Care and Ethics Committee at Affiliated Eye Hospital of Nanchang University and conducted according to the ARVO Statement for the Use of Animals in Ophthalmic and Vision Research. The animals were housed under standard conditions and maintained in temperature-controlled rooms with a normal 12-hour light/12-hour dark cycle.

sec.title: Primary Astrocyte Culture and Activation
sec.p: The whole brains of postnatal days 2–3 C57BL/6 mice were dissected, and the cerebral cortices were isolated and transferred to a prepared 2 mg/mL papain solution for digestion.13,19,24 The obtained cell suspension was passed through a 40-µm cell strainer and spun in a centrifuge at 1000g for three minutes. The pellets were resuspended in basic culture medium and cultured for 24 hours, after which the medium was changed to enrichment medium. After the cells reached confluence, the medium was changed to maintenance medium, and the cells were cultured for three days. The TIC cytokine cocktail was prepared by adding 3 ng/mL IL-1α (I3901; Sigma-Aldrich Corp., St. Louis, MO, USA), 400 ng/mL C1q (MBS143105 or MBS147305; MyBioSource, San Diego, CA, USA), and 30 ng/mL TNF (210-TA-020; R&D Systems, Minneapolis, MN, USA) to the maintenance medium. Primary astrocytes were then treated with the TIC cocktail for 24 hours.

sec.title: Construction of Lentiviral Vectors and Lentivirus Transfection
sec.p: To generate lentiviruses expressing shRNA specific to mouse SIRT4, the shRNA sequence targeting mouse SIRT4 (5′-TGGAGAGTTGCTGCCTTTAAT-3′) was designed using the RNAiDesigner program (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). A negative control construct (scrambled shRNA) was generated from a non-targeting sequence. These sequences were cloned into the hU6-MCS-CBh-gcGFP-IRES-puromycin lentiviral vector (GeneChem, Shanghai, China). The recombinant lentiviral vectors were co-transfected with packaging plasmids (psPAX2 and pMD2.G) into 293T cells. After 72 hours, the lentivirus-containing supernatant was collected and filtered through a 0.45-µm filter. Target cells were seeded in complete medium at a density of 3 × 10⁴ cells/mL and incubated for 16 hours. Lentivirus was then added at a multiplicity of infection of 100, along with 20 µL of HiTransG P infection enhancement solution per well. After 72 hours, infection efficiency was assessed by GFP fluorescence, and cells were used for subsequent experiments.

sec.title: Retinal Ischemia/Reperfusion Model and Resveratrol Treatment
sec.p: The mice were anesthetized with 2% isoflurane with an oxygen flow rate of 0.5 L/min, and mydriasis was induced using tropicamide eye drops. A 32-gauge needle was inserted into the anterior chamber at the corneal margin, carefully avoiding the iris and lens. A saline solution reservoir was elevated to 150 cm (corresponding to 110 mm Hg) and connected to the needle for 60 minutes to elevate intraocular pressure. Intraocular pressure was monitored throughout the procedure. Sham-operated mice underwent the same surgical procedure without anterior chamber cannulation. After surgery, levofloxacin eye drops were administered three times daily until euthanasia. Vital signs and ocular conditions were monitored daily. On postoperative days 1, 3, and 7, mice were euthanized by intraperitoneal injection of 1% (w/v) pentobarbital sodium solution (overdose). Optic nerve tissues from both groups were collected for further analysis.

Resveratrol is a nonspecific activator of the sirtuin family. Previous studies have shown that resveratrol can activate SIRT4.22 In this study, resveratrol was used as a pharmacological treatment to investigate the role of SIRT4. Six- to eight-week–old wild-type (WT) and SIRT4-KO mice were intraperitoneally injected with resveratrol (20 mg/kg) for five consecutive days before I/R induction, with an additional dose administered on the day of surgery. The control group received an equal volume of vehicle (DMSO diluted with normal saline solution).

sec.title: Fixation, Sectioning, and Immunofluorescence Staining
sec.p: Mice were euthanized by intraperitoneal injection of 80 mg/kg pentobarbital sodium. The eyeballs were enucleated, fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, and submitted to Servicebio (Wuhan, China) for paraffin embedding and sectioning. Cross-sections (5 µm thick) were prepared through the optic nerve head. Cells grown on coverslips and tissue sections were permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100 (Solarbio, Beijing, China) in PBS for 10 minutes and blocked in PBS containing 5% donkey serum for one hour at room temperature. The sections were incubated with primary antibodies overnight at 4°C. The working dilutions and sources of the antibodies used are listed in Table 1. The following day, the sections were incubated with secondary antibodies at room temperature for one hour in the dark. Subsequently, the sections were counterstained with 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (Boster, Wuhan, China) for 15 minutes and examined microscope (Zeiss, Göttingen, Germany). At least three retinal sections from different mice per group were used for analysis.

sec.title: Retinal Flattening and Immunofluorescence Staining
sec.p: The retinas were cut into a four-leaf shape and incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies against RBPMS (ab152101, 1:200; Abcam, Cambridge, MA, USA), and then incubated with AlexaFluor 594-conjugated anti-rabbit IgG (ab150080, 1:200; Abcam) at room temperature in the dark for one hour. After mounting with antifade reagent, the retinal whole mounts were imaged under a fluorescence microscope, and high-magnification images were acquired. Images were collected at the periphery (approximately 150–200 µm from the retinal edge), middle (approximately 700–800 µm from the edge), and center (approximately 1500–1600 µm from the edge) of each quadrant.25 A total of 12 images were collected per retina. Finally, RBPMS-positive RGCs were counted using ImageJ software.

sec.title: Western Blot Analysis
sec.p: Retinal tissue and rMC-1 cells were lysed in RIPA buffer supplemented with protease inhibitors (100:1, v/v) on ice for 30 minutes. The lysate was subsequently spun in a centrifuge at 12,000 rpm for 15 minutes at 4°C. The supernatant was collected, mixed with loading buffer, and transferred to microcentrifuge tubes. Protein concentration was determined using a TGem microspectrophotometer (Tiangen, Beijing, China) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Protein samples (25 µg) were separated by electrophoresis on a 10% SDS–polyacrylamide gel and transferred to PVDF membranes. The membranes were blocked with 5% skim milk (Servicebio; GC310001) for one hour at room temperature, incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies, and then incubated with secondary antibodies for one hour at room temperature. Signals were detected using a chemiluminescence imaging system. Band intensity was quantified using ImageJ software.

sec.title: Phosphatidylcholine Determination
sec.p: The phosphatidylcholine colorimetric assay kit (E-BC-K796-M; Elabscience, Wuhan, China) was used. Cell samples were diluted at a ratio of 1 × 10⁶ cells per 0.2 mL of reagent I (1:200, v/v). The lysate was then spun in a centrifuge at 4°C and 10,000g for 10 minutes, and the supernatant was collected for analysis. Culture medium samples were spun in a centrifuge at 4°C and 10,000g for 10 minutes, and the resulting supernatant was directly used for analysis without additional reagent addition.

sec.title: Long-Chain Fatty Acids Determination
sec.p: First, 50 mg of the sample was carefully homogenized. After homogenization, the sample was vortexed (2500 r/min, 10 minutes), ultrasonicated (4°C, 15 minutes), and spun in a centrifuge (4200 r/min, five min, 4°C), and the supernatant was carefully collected, leaving the pellet. A solution of NaOH-MeOH (200 µL, 0.05 mol/L) was then added to 500 µL of the supernatant before carefully solidifying by exposing to liquid nitrogen. Next, an additional solution of NaOH-MeOH (400 µL, 0.4 mol/L) was added to the solidified sample and allowed to react for 10 minutes at 70°C. The resulting product was later placed in an ice bath to cool down. Concurrently, dichloromethane and deionized water were added to the resulting product and vortexed (2500 r/min, five min), to allow for low temperature phase separation (4200 r/min, five minutes, 4°C). 300 µL of the organic phase was carefully aspirated, and 300 µL of HCl-MeOH acidic solution was added. The sample was made to undergo a thermodynamic equilibrium treatment at 70 oC. After the end of the reaction, 500 µL of n-Hexane and 300 µL of deionized water were added to the resulting sample and centrifuged to allow for a phase separation. 200 µL of the upper layer (n-Hexane) of the phase separated sample was carefully collected and stored at −20°C for further analysis. GC-MS analysis was performed in static ion scan mode; the data were analyzed using chromatography.

sec.title: ATP Determination
sec.p: After the cells were collected, they were resuspended in lysis buffer (approximately 200-300 µL for every 2 × 106 cells) and homogenized for about five minutes. The mixture was then boiled for two minutes and cooled under running water. Subsequently, it was spun in a centrifuge at 4°C and 10,000g for 10 to 15 minutes. The supernatant was collected, and the ATP content was measured using an ATP content detection kit (G4309; Servicebio, Wuhan, China).

sec.title: Data Analysis
sec.p: All quantified data are from at least three independent experiments. Unless otherwise specified, each sample comprised 15 optic nerves pooled from 15 mice (only the right eye of each mouse was used for subsequent experiments). All results are presented as the mean ± SEM. Statistical analyses were performed using ImageJ and GraphPad Prism 7.0 software. To determine statistical significance, an unpaired Student's t-test was used for comparisons between two groups, and one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post hoc test was used for comparisons among three or more groups. P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

sec.title: SIRT4 Is Highly Expressed on Glial Cells
sec.p: To explore the impact of SIRT4 deficiency on the optic nerve of mice, the parental generation was produced by targeted knockout of exons 3 and 4 of the SIRT4 gene, and sufficient offspring were generated through mating of the parental generation (Fig. 1A). PCR was used to identify the gene phenotype of SIRT4 KO and WT offspring mice, and successful knockout of the SIRT4 gene was confirmed (Fig. 1B). Western blotting of optic nerve proteins from two-month-old SIRT4 KO and WT mice showed that SIRT4 was almost undetectable in the optic nerve of SIRT4 KO mice (Fig. 1D). GFAP-labeled astrocytes22 are distributed in the retina, optic disc, and optic nerve, whereas GS-labeled retinal Müller glial cells23 are widely distributed throughout the retinal structure. Immunofluorescence staining of retinal tissue demonstrated that SIRT4-positive cells were distributed across all layers of the retina, extending from the outer nuclear layer (ONL) to the inner limiting membrane. SIRT4 staining mostly co-localized with GS staining, while only a small amount co-localized with GFAP staining. The co-localization signals were predominantly observed in the cytoplasm of Müller glial cells adjacent to the ganglion cell layer, and were also detected in the cytoplasm of retinal astrocytes. These results indicated that SIRT4 was mainly distributed in Müller glial cells and astrocytes in retinal tissue (Fig. 1E). SIRT4-positive cells were distributed across all layers of the optic disc and optic nerve, and SIRT4 immunostaining exhibited strong co-localization with GFAP, predominantly within astrocytes located in these regions (Fig. 1E). To further validate whether SIRT4 was expressed in astrocytes, we performed immunofluorescence co-staining for SIRT4 and GFAP in primary astrocytes. The results demonstrated a significant co-localization of GFAP-labeled red fluorescence and SIRT4-labeled green fluorescence within these cells (Fig. 1C). These results indicated that SIRT4 was mainly distributed in astrocytes in the retina, optic disc and optic nerve, as well as Müller glial cells in the retina. However, after SIRT4 gene knockout, the expression of GFAP in the optic disc, retina, and optic nerve was significantly reduced, and retinal GS expression was also diminished (Fig. 1E).

sec.title: SIRT4 Exerted a Protective Effect Against RGCs injury Caused by the I/R Model
sec.p: In this study, the retinal plain films were immunofluorescence-labeled using the RGCs-specific marker RBPMS (Fig. 2). The left side of Figure 2A presented a schematic diagram of a complete retinal patch centered on the optic disc. The retina was divided into four quadrants, each of which included three regions: proximal, central and peripheral. One day after injury in the wild-type mouse I/R model, the number of RBPMS-labeled RGCs significantly decreased in the proximal and central regions of the retina, whereas no obvious change was observed in the distal retina (Figs. 2A; 2C). In the WT mouse I/R model, the number of RGCs labeled by RBPMS in each retinal region was significantly reduced at both three and seven days after injury, with a more pronounced decrease observed at seven days (Figs. 2A; 2C). To investigate the effect of SIRT4 on RGCs and their axonal injuries in the I/R model, we performed I/R injury treatment on SIRT4-KO mice. The experimental results showed that compared to the WT mice subjected to seven-day I/R injury, the number of RGCs in the retina of SIRT4-KO mice was significantly reduced at seven days after injury (Figs. 2A, 2B, 2D). However, in the case of simple SIRT4 knockout without induced damage, the number of RGCs across the entire retina did not change significantly (Figs. 2A, 2B, 2D). Therefore we draw the following conclusion: SIRT4 gene knockout has no significant effect on RGCs and their axons under normal conditions, but it aggravates the degree of damage to RGCs and their axons in the I/R injury model. To further explore the potential protective effect of SIRT4 in RGCs and axonal injury, we overexpressed SIRT4 using the Sirtuins family agonist resveratrol. The research results indicated that resveratrol treatment has no effect on the number of RGCs in the retina of each region, but it significantly attenuated the damage of RGCs in the retina of each region caused by the I/R model for 7 days (Figs. 2A, 2B, 2D). Collectively, these results suggest that SIRT4 exerts a protective effect against RGCs and optic nerve injury in retinal I/R injury models.

sec.title: Non-Targeted Metabolomics Analysis and Transcriptomic Analysis of WT and SIRT4-KO Groups
sec.p: In the previous results, we found that SIRT4 has a protective effect on RGCs and the optic nerve, but its specific mechanism of action remains unclear. To explore the specific protective mechanism of SIRT4 on the optic nerve, we conducted non-targeted metabolic sequencing analyses and transcriptomic analysis of the optic nerves in the WT and SIRT4-KO groups. Based on the results of OPLS-DA, the subsequent analysis of differential metabolites is reliable (Supplementary Fig. S1A). A total of 1156 metabolites were detected in this study, among which 106 metabolites exhibited significant differences between the WT and SIRT4-KO groups. Compared with the WT group, 77 differential metabolites were significantly upregulated and 29 differential metabolites were significantly downregulated in the SIRT4-KO group (Supplementary Fig. S1C). Through the analysis of differential metabolites, we found that compared with the WT group, the levels of PC, one LCFA and lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) were significantly increased in the SIRT4-KO group (Fig. 3A; Table 2).To clarify the metabolic pathways involved, a systematic analysis of the differential metabolites was conducted based on the KEGG database. The results showed that these differential metabolites were involved in multiple key cellular processes, including but not limited to cell growth and death, substance transport, and metabolic regulation pathways. In addition, they were also involved in information processing processes related to molecular signal transduction, signal transduction mechanisms, and cell membrane transport. Further research indicated that these differential metabolites are closely associated with a variety of human diseases, such as neurodegenerative diseases, endocrine and metabolic disorders, and cardiovascular diseases. These findings further suggest that SIRT4 may have an impact on the pathogenesis of glaucoma neurodegeneration. Meanwhile, SIRT4 is also involved in metabolism and biological system pathways. A variety of differential metabolites are widely involved in multiple key areas such as nucleotide metabolism, amino acid metabolism, cofactor and vitamin metabolism, lipid metabolism, and energy metabolism (Fig. 3B). It can be found from the Circos circle diagram that there is a close correlation among various differentially expressed metabolites (Supplementary Fig. S1B). To further validate the changes of PC levels, we detected the PC content in the optic nerves of mice from both the WT group and the SIRT4-KO group using colorimetry assays. The results showed that a significant increase in PC levels in the SIRT4-KO group compared to the WT group (Fig. 3C). To further explore through which genes SIRT4 exerts its protective mechanism on the optic nerve, we conducted transcriptomic analyses of the optic nerve in the WT and SIRT4-KO groups.

sec.p: A total of 23,932 genes were analyzed, and 239 significantly differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified, including 149 upregulated and 90 downregulated genes. Samples from the WT group and the SIRT4-KO group were separated as shown by 2DPCA plots (Supplementary Fig. S1D). The 15 up-regulated/down-regulated genes with the greatest differentially multiples were represented using differentially gene radar maps (Supplementary Fig. S1E). Clustered heat maps of 55 DEGs associated with neuroprotection revealed significant alterations in gene expression within the optic nerve following SIRT4 gene knockout compared to the WT group. Notably, increased expression levels were observed for APOL6, Apolipoprotein L9a (APOL9a), and Apolipoprotein L9b (APOL9b; Fig. 3D; Table 3). In the glaucoma microbead-induced ocular hypertension model, comparative analysis of samples collected at 7 days versus 0 days revealed that Apol9b24 was among the top 30 genes most significantly upregulated in ONH astrocytes. Through KEGG enrichment analysis, we found that the DEGs were significantly enriched in signaling pathways associated with human diseases following SIRT4 gene knockout. Specifically, this change impacts viral infection pathways involving multiple pathogens, including Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus, herpes simplex virus, human T-cell leukemia virus, Epstein-Barr virus, human papillomavirus, prions, and SARS-CoV-2. In addition, it involves pathways related to influenza A, hepatitis C, hepatitis B, lipid metabolism and atherosclerosis, diabetes, Cushing's syndrome and urticaria. The deletion of the SIRT4 gene may also interfere with viral carcinogenicity and the regulatory mechanism of Staphylococcus aureus infection. Furthermore, SIRT4 knockout affects a variety of bioinformatics pathways, including neuroactive ligand-receptor interactions, cytokine-cytokine receptor interactions, and further affects organic compound signaling pathways such as the estrogen signaling pathway and Toll-like receptor signaling pathway (Fig. 3E). In the GO enrichment bar chart, significant enrichment was also observed in pathways such as neuroprotection and lipid metabolism (Supplementary Fig. S1F). To validate the results of transcriptome sequencing, qRT-PCR was used to assess the expression levels of six neuroprotection-related genes. After SIRT4 gene knockout, increased expression was observed in APOL6, adiponectin (C1Q and collagen domain containing, Adipoq), calcium homeostasis modulator 6 (CALHM6), cholesterol 25-hydroxylase (CH25H), and fibroblast growth factor 4 (FGF4), whereas a decreased expression level was detected for Wnt family member 7A (WNT7A) (Figs. 3F–K).

sec.title: Transcriptomic Analysis of SIRT4-KO and SIRT4-KO I/R 7d Groups and Combined Analysis of Non-Targeted Metabolomics and Transcriptomics
sec.p: To explore the gene changes under I/R injury conditions, we adopted transcriptomic analysis methods to systematically study the gene expression profiles of the optic nerve in WT mice seven days after injury in the I/R model. It can be observed that, compared with the WT group, the expression of neuroprotection-related genes in the optic nerve seven days after injury in the I/R model showed significant differences. Moreover, the expression levels of APOC1, APOOL, APOO, APOA2 and APOB in apolipoproteins were upregulated, whereas those of APOA4, APOC3 and APOLD1 were downregulated (Supplementary Fig. S2, Supplementary Table S1). To further explore the specific target genes of SIRT4 in the protective effect of I/R injury, we conducted transcriptomic analysis on the optic nerve of the SIRT4-KO mouse I/R model seven days after injury. A total of 24,086 genes were analyzed, and 3810 were identified as significantly differentially expressed, including 2409 upregulated and 1401 downregulated genes. Among these, 52 DEGs associated with neuroprotection were identified in the I/R injury model in SIRT4-KO mice. Clustering heatmaps revealed distinct gene expression patterns in the optic nerve of SIRT4-KO mice seven days after I/R injury compared to the control SIRT4-KO group, indicating a significant transcriptional response after injury. Interestingly, we found a decreased levels of apolipoproteins APOA4, APOA1, APOF, APOL19a, APOL19b, and APOL6, along with increased levels of apolipoproteins APOO, APOOL and APOC4 (Fig. 4A; Table 4). In combination with the previous results, the increase of APOL6, APOL9a and APOL19b in the SIRT4 gene after knockout compared with the WT group (Fig. 3D; Table 4), the changes of these three genes after optic nerve injury in the SIRT4-KO group of mice in the I/R model are reversed, and the specific mechanism remain to be explored. KEGG enrichment analysis of DEGs demonstrated that in the I/R injury model of SIRT4-KO mice, DEGs were mainly enriched in signal pathways related to environmental information processing, human diseases, and organic systems. These genes were significantly involved in cellular environmental information processing processes such as the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway, neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction, MAPK signaling pathway, Ras signaling pathway, and Rap1 signaling pathway. In addition, these DEGs also affected pathways related to herpes simplex virus type 1 infection, human papillomavirus infection and Salmonella infection, and were closely associated with proteoglycan, lipid metabolism and disease pathways such as atherosclerosis and tuberculosis in cancer. At the same time, these genes were also implicated in organic system-related pathways such as chemokine metabolism pathways, axon guidance, and retrograde endogenous cannabinoid signaling (Fig. 4B). GO enrichment analysis revealed that the DEGs were significantly enriched in multiple biological process pathways, including the positive regulation of nuclear division, regulation of responses to external stimuli, synaptic tissue construction, muscle tissue development, ameba-like cell migration, and negative regulation of immune system processes. Additionally, these genes were also prominently associated with various cellular component categories, including synaptic membranes, complex receptors, extracellular matrix containing collagen, chromosomal regions, and postsynaptic membranes (Fig. 4C). To further explore the mechanism by which SIRT4 protects the optic nerve, we conducted a combined analysis of the non-targeted metabolic sequencing and transcriptional sequencing used in the WT group and the SIRT4-KO group in this study. Analysis revealed that after SIRT4 knockout, the DEGs and metabolites were significantly enriched in the neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction pathway, and had an impact on the NoD-like receptor signaling pathway, cAMP signaling pathway, and neurodegenerative disease-related signaling pathways. This result further validates the key role of SIRT4 in the protective mechanism against neurodegeneration in I/R model (Figs. 4D–G).

sec.title: SIRT4 Knockout Exacerbates Ischemia/Reperfusion-Induced Injury
sec.p: In previous studies, we demonstrated that SIRT4 exerts a protective effect on RGCs and their axons. Furthermore, integrated metabolomics and transcriptomics analysis led us to hypothesize that the neuroprotective mechanism of SIRT4 may involve its regulation of astrocyte mitochondrial-associated apolipoproteins and the LCFAs and PCs they carry. To further validate these findings, we established I/R injury models in WT mice at multiple time points. Western blotting analysis revealed that both SIRT4 and OPA1 proteins peaked on day 1 after injury, subsequently declined gradually, and were significantly reduced by day 7, exhibiting a synchronized dynamic pattern. In contrast, APOL6 expression was significantly decreased on day 1 and markedly increased by day 7, displaying an inverse trend relative to SIRT4 (Figs. 5A–C, 5E). Immunofluorescence staining of the optic disc, retina and optic nerve revealed decreased expression of SIRT4 in all three locations on the seventh day after I/R model injury, consistent with Western blotting results (Fig. 5H). GBP2 is a protein specifically upregulated in reactive astrocytes of both mice and humans under pathological conditions.3,25 Western blotting analysis showed a significant increase in GBP2 on days 3 and 7 after I/R injury (Figs. 5A, 5D), suggesting that I/R model injury may induce the development of neurotoxic reactive astrocyte phenotypes. By detecting mitochondrial dynamics-related proteins, we observed that MFN2 was significantly reduced on the 3rd and 7th days (Figs. 5A, 5F), accompanied by a significant increase in FIS1 on the same days (Figs. 5A, 5G), coinciding with a tendency toward mitochondrial fission. To investigate whether LCFAs are associated with RGCs death in the glaucoma I/R model, we performed mass spectrometry analysis to measure 28 kinds of LCFAs in the optic nerves of WT and SIRT4-KO mice on the seventh day of the I/R model. Our results showed that I/R injury led to elevated LCFA levels in the optic nerves of WT mice, whereas no significant change was observed in SIRT4-KO mice (Fig. 5I). These findings indicate that SIRT4 does not exert its protective effect on RGCs through modulation of LCFA metabolism. On the day 7 after injury in the I/R model, a significant reduction in SIRT4 expression was observed, accompanied by a neurotoxic phenotype in astrocytes. Therefore day 7 was selected as the time point for constructing I/R models in both WT and SIRT4-KO mice. Western blotting analysis revealed that APOL6 protein expression was upregulated following SIRT4 knockout. Similarly, I/R injury alone increased APOL6 expression, and this increase was further exacerbated by SIRT4 gene deletion (Figs. 5J, 5K). GBP2 protein expression did not significantly change following SIRT4-KO, but was markedly upregulated after I/R injury, with a more pronounced increase observed in the SIRT4-KO group compared to controls (Figs. 5J, 5L). Concurrently, the expression levels of mitochondrial fusion proteins OPA1 and MFN2 gradually decreased, whereas the expression of the mitochondrial fission protein FIS1 increased (Figs. 5M–O). To further assess mitochondrial function and morphology alterations under these conditions, we performed transmission electron microscopy to observe the mitochondrial morphology of astrocytes in the optic nerve. In the WT group, astrocyte mitochondria exhibited normal morphology with well-defined cristae. In contrast, the SIRT4-KO group displayed mild mitochondrial matrix swelling, thinning of the intracristal space, and shortened, swollen cristae. In the WT group, most mitochondria exhibited significant swelling seven days after I/R injury, accompanied by localized dissolution of the intracellular matrix and reduction and disappearance of the cristae. In the SIRT4-KO group, after I/R injury, mitochondria displayed a tendency toward fission, with smaller size, reduced or absent cristae, membrane protrusions, structural damage, matrix effusion, and the presence of lipid inclusions (Fig. 5P). In summary, mitochondrial damage was relatively mild in the SIRT4-KO group under baseline conditions but worsened following I/R injury; however, compared to the WT group, the extent of damage was more pronounced, indicating that SIRT4 deficiency exacerbates mitochondrial injury in the context of I/R.

sec.title: SIRT4 Knockdown Enhances Astrocyte Toxic Activation Caused by TIC Models
sec.p: To further investigate whether SIRT4 causes damage to RGCs and their axons by mediating the neurotoxic phenotype of astrocytes, we constructed an in vitro TIC-induced activation model using primary astrocytes. Western blotting analysis revealed increased SIRT4 protein expression 24 hours after TIC injury (Fig. 6A), along with upregulated GBP2 protein levels (Fig. 6C). Immunofluorescence results showed enhanced expression of both SIRT4 and GFAP after TIC injury (Fig. 6G), coinciding with the acquisition of a neurotoxic astrocytic phenotype. In contrast to SIRT4, APOL6 protein expression was reduced (Fig. 6B). Additionally, the levels of mitochondrial fusion proteins OPA1 and MFN2, as well as the mitochondrial fission protein FIS1, were decreased (Figs. 6D–F). To further validate the role of SIRT4 in astrocytes, we knocked down SIRT4 using lentiviral transduction, achieving a transfection efficiency exceeding 95% (Fig. 6H). Subsequently, we constructed a TIC injury model based on that. Western blotting analysis revealed that SIRT4 protein expression was significantly reduced in the SIRT4 RNAi lentivirus group (shSIRT4 group) compared to the normal control group (NC group) (Fig. 7I). Notably, SIRT4 knockdown led to increased GBP2 protein expression, induced reactive astrogliosis, and exacerbated neurotoxic responses following TIC-induced injury (Figs. 6J, 6L). Furthermore, APOL6 protein levels were upregulated upon SIRT4 depletion (Figs. 6J, 6K), whereas the expression of mitochondrial dynamics-related proteins progressively decreased (Figs. 6J, 6M–O). To assess mitochondrial function, ATP levels in astrocytes across different experimental groups were measured using chemiluminescence. The results showed that a significant decrease in ATP levels under TIC injury conditions, with a more pronounced reduction observed after SIRT4 knockdown (Fig. 6P), indicating that SIRT4 deficiency exacerbates mitochondrial dysfunction in astrocytes induced by TIC. To verify whether SIRT4 mediates RGCs and axonal damage caused by PC carried by apolipoproteins secreted by neurotoxic astrocytes, we quantified PC levels in both astrocytes and their astrocyte-conditioned medium (ACM) in the NC and shSIRT4 groups under TIC injury using colorimetry. Although intracellular PC content did not differ significantly between groups (Fig. 6Q), PC levels in the ACM were markedly elevated upon SIRT4 knockdown. Notably, TIC injury alone did not increase PC secretion, whereas the combination of TIC injury and SIRT4 knockdown led to a substantial increase in extracellular PC (Fig. 6R). Given the known neurotoxic effects of PC, this suggests enhanced potential for neuronal damage under these conditions. Therefore we speculate that SIRT4 knockdown increases the susceptibility of astrocytes to TIC-induced injury and may promote neurodegeneration by facilitating the release of toxic PC species.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this study, we found that SIRT4 is highly expressed in retinal Müller glial cells as well as in astrocytes of the retina, optic nerve head and optic nerve. SIRT4 exerts a protective effect against RGCs injury caused by the I/R model. The injury of the I/R model induces neurotoxic phenotypes in astrocytes of the optic nerve, disrupts mitochondrial morphology and function of astrocytes, and increase the secretion of LCFA. However, the secretion of LCFA has no direct relationship with SIRT4 knockdown. The mitochondrial structure and function in astrocytes of the optic nerve were slightly impaired in SIRT4-KO mice, accompanied by reduced ATP levels, elevated phosphatidylcholine, and increased expression of apolipoprotein APOL6. Moreover, SIRT4-KO would aggravate the mitochondrial damage and increase the expression of APOL6 caused by the I/R model. Knockdown of SIRT4 in astrocytes would exacerbate the neurotoxic phenotype induced by the TIC model in astrocytes and cause mitochondrial dysfunction in astrocytes. Concurrently, this process promoted increased secretion of phosphatidylcholine into ACM, which may contribute to RGC injury and axonal degeneration. In conclusion, SIRT4 exerts a protective effect on RGCs and their axons by modulating astrocytic mitochondrial function and regulating the transport of long-chain fatty acids and phosphatidylcholine via apolipoprotein APOL6.

In this study, we observed an intriguing phenomenon: following SIRT4 knockout, there was a marked increase in apolipoproteins such as APOL6 (Fig. 3D; Table 2), along with elevated levels of LCFAs and PC (Fig. 3A; Table 1), despite the absence of damage to RGCs or the optic nerve (Fig. 2). This appears inconsistent with previous findings showing that reactive astrocytes induce fat apoptosis and damage to neurons via long-chain saturated free fatty acids and phosphatidylcholine carried by APOE and APOJ.17 However, in constructing our in vitro glaucoma injury model, we observed that SIRT4 knockdown significantly exacerbates the detrimental effects of PC on RGCs. This observation can be plausibly explained by the cryptic phenotypes associated with Sirtuins family gene knockout. Specifically, SIRT4 deficiency may trigger compensatory upregulation of other Sirtuins family members. Evidence from SIRT4-KO mouse models indicates marked increases in SIRT1 and SIRT3 expression levels.26,27 Given the functional overlap within the Sirtuins family, we hypothesize that such compensatory upregulation may partially offset the functional impairments resulting from SIRT4 loss. This mechanism may account for the absence of pronounced phenotypic abnormalities under normal physiological conditions. Nevertheless, under specific pathological or stress conditions, this compensation may prove insufficient, thereby unmasking the distinct and essential roles of SIRT4 in certain biological contexts. In summary, our findings suggest that SIRT4 may regulate GS expression in retinal Müller glial cells and GFAP expression in astrocytes of the optic disc, retina, and optic nerve—providing a foundation for future investigations into SIRT4 function in optic nerve and optic disc astrocytes, although the underlying molecular mechanisms require further cellular-level validation.

This study found that SIRT4 exerts a protective effect on RGCs and their axons by regulating mitochondrial function in astrocytes. It reveals a close association between abnormal axonal energy metabolism in RGCs and neurodegeneration driven by mitochondrial dysfunction in retinal I/R model.28,29 Structural abnormalities of mitochondria in ONH astrocytes, along with RGC and axonal pathology, serve as clear indicators of this underlying dysfunction.30 Previous studies have shown that ONH astrocytes can transfer healthy mitochondria to axons. Under injury conditions, astrocytes can transfer healthy mitochondria to neurons, which serves as an important mechanism to enhance their survival rate.12,31,32 In this study, SIRT4 gene knockout significantly exacerbated mitochondrial damage in astrocytes in the I/R model (Fig. 5), so we hypothesized that SIRT4 deficiency may impair the ability of astrocytes to deliver healthy mitochondria to RGCs or optic nerve, thereby further aggravating I/R-induced damage. Liddelow et al.3 demonstrated that a cytokine mixture consisting of TNF-α, IL-1α, and C1q, released by activated microglia, can directly induce a shift in astrocyte populations toward neurotoxic phenotypes. This astrocyte subtype is characterized by upregulated expression of C3 and GBP2, which serve as established molecular markers.3,33,34 The study showed that the immunoreactivity of GBP2 was almost entirely co-localized with that of GFAP-positive astrocytes.24 In this study, we found that GBP2 protein expression was significantly elevated on the third and seventh days after I/R injury in the in vivo model (Fig. 5), and similarly, astrocytes in the in vitro model exhibited increased GBP2 protein expression after TIC injury (Fig. 6). Notably, SIRT4 gene knockout further enhanced GBP2 expression in both the I/R and TIC injury models (Figs. 5, 6), suggesting that SIRT4 deficiency exacerbates the development of neurotoxic astrocyte phenotypes in response to diverse neuronal insults. Therefore these findings underscore the importance of studying neurotoxic astrocytes to elucidate the neuroprotective mechanisms mediated by SIRT4.

The results of Western blotting in this study showed a significant reduction in SIRT4 expression on the seventh day of injury in the I/R model, accompanied by a consistent and marked reduction in T-OPA1 levels (Fig. 5). Genetic knockout or knockdown of SIRT4 exacerbated the injury and led to a decrease in OPA1 protein expression (Figs. 5, 6). These findings align with our previous observations showing that SIRT4 protects Müller glial cells through regulation of OPA1.21 OPA1 protein is widely distributed in the ONH of rats and humans, as well as in the mitochondria of RGCs in the retinas of mice, rats and humans.35,36 Therefore, in this study, OPA1 changes dynamically with SIRT4, further confirming the protective effect of SIRT4 on RGCs and astrocytes. We further explored whether SIRT4 exerts a protective effect on the I/R injury model by regulating astrocyte mitochondrial kinetic proteins. SIRT4 overexpression was found to significantly induce densification of the mitochondrial network structure and increase the average mitochondrial length.20 Further mechanism studies revealed that SIRT4 directly interacts with the key mitochondrial fusion protein L-OPA1 through its enzymatic catalytic activity, thereby regulating the dynamic mitochondrial fusion process.37 These findings are consistent with the results of the present study, which demonstrated that knockdown or knockout of SIRT4 significantly reduced the expression levels of mitochondrial fusion-related proteins OPA1 and MFN2, while markedly increasing the expression of the mitochondrial fission-related protein FIS1 (Figs. 5, 6). In addition, electron microscopy observations further confirmed that the reduction of SIRT4 would lead to a tendency of astrocyte mitochondria to divide (Fig. 5).

Non-targeted metabolomics revealed that SIRT4 knockout reduced ATP levels in the optic nerve (Fig. 3; Table 1), and SIRT4 knockdown exacerbated damage in the TIC model, leading to decreased ATP production in astrocytes (Fig. 6). The susceptibility to optic nerve metabolism and chronic metabolic stress were particularly significant in the DBA/2J glaucoma mouse model, specifically manifested as decreased ATP levels, reduced substrate availability, down-regulation of transport protein expression, and mitochondrial dysfunction.38 A recently published study shows that mitochondrial anterograde transport is significantly reduced in mouse microbead models, resulting in a decrease in ATP levels within axons.39 Astrocytes mainly generate ATP through the glycolytic pathway, although this pathway yields relatively little ATP, it generates lactate as a byproduct. Lactate serves as an important energy substrate and is transferred to neurons through the astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle, supporting neuronal energy demands.40,41 Although SIRT4 knockout mice often exhibit occult phenotypes, studies have shown that the absence of SIRT4 has an impact on key metabolic activities, including amino acids and fatty acid metabolism, as well as ATP homeostasis.42 These studies are in line with our results, with impaired mitochondrial function and reduced ATP synthesis in astrocytes after SIRT4-KO.

Through non-targeted metabolic sequencing, we found that PC increased in the optic nerve after SIRT4-KO, which was further validated by colorimetric assays (Fig. 3). Significant activation of astrocytes was observed in the glial lamina of the optic nerve in glaucoma patients, accompanied by randomly distributed oxygen-loving lipid substances, including exudates, cell protrusions, and lipid droplet structures,43 indicating extensive damage to mitochondrial function in optic nerve axons.43 In hyperactive neurons, lipid accumulation is toxic, not only due to the high sensitivity of these lipids to peroxidation but also possibly involving other potential mechanisms of cellular damage.44 Studies have found that in the cell membranes of reactive astrocytes, phosphatidylcholine containing very long-chain fatty acid acyl chains (very long-chain phosphatidylcholine) is significantly upregulated; while in reactive ACM, phosphatidylcholine containing long-chain saturated free FFAs shows a significant upward trend.17 Moreover, lipid particles reconstituted from reactive astrocyte ACM and its lipid components exhibit toxic effects on RGCs in vitro, further confirming the known high sensitivity of RGCs to fat toxicity.45 Long-chain free FFAs and PC are partially involved in the mediation of RGCs toxicity after axonal injury.17 Our research results are highly consistent with these studies. After knocking down SIRT4, we constructed a reactive astrocyte model with TIC injury and found that neither TIC injury nor SIRT4 knockdown caused significant changes in PC in astrocytes. At this time, astrocytes secrete a substantial amount of PC, and consistent with this, PC levels in reactive ACM were significantly elevated after SIRT4 knockdown. These findings indicate that SIRT4 deficiency promotes the release of excessive toxic lipid species from reactive astrocytes, contributing to RGC and optic nerve damage, ultimately resulting in RGC degeneration and loss. Moreover, both astrocytes and microglia are involved in the secretion and degradation of a large amount of lipids.46 Further investigation into lipid-mediated functions (such as lipid droplet formation) may be of great significance for studying the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases.

In this study, we found an increase in APOL6 gene expression after SIRT4-KO, which was confirmed by PCR, along with a significant upregulation of APOL6 protein levels (Fig. 3A; Table 2). In contrast, in the SIRT4-KO I/R model, the expression of APOL6 gene decreased 7 days after injury (Fig. 5A; Table 3), while the expression of APOL6 protein increased. We analyzed three possible reasons for the inconsistent gene and protein results: first, the temporal differences in gene and protein expression; second, the fine-tuning of translation efficiency; and third, protein stability and post-translational modifications. In reactive astrocyte ACM, a significant enrichment of lipid proteins APOE and APOJ was observed, which may suggest a change in the lipid effloression function of astrocytes.17 Apolipoproteins (such as APOE, APOL6, etc.) may play a key role in maintaining neuronal health by promoting the transfer of FAs from neurons to astrocytes. Based on these findings, we hypothesize that SIRT4 knockdown or knockout impairs ApoL6-mediated transport of long-chain fatty acids and phosphatidylcholines from neurons to astrocytes, leading to intracellular lipid accumulation. This effect is more pronounced in particular under conditions of retianl I/R injury, where increased lipid accumulation exacerbates lipid toxicity and/or lipid peroxidation damage. With the reduction of SIRT4 protein, there was an increase in APOL6 protein expression, showing opposite trends (Figs. 5, 6). This phenomenon may be attributed to three potential mechanisms. First, an indirect regulatory mechanism: APOL6 and SIRT4 may coexist within a larger protein complex or shared signaling pathway, and the absence of SIRT4 could exert a negative regulatory influence on APOL6 within this context. Second, a feedback regulation mechanism: cellular sensing of SIRT4 functional deficiency after knockout may trigger compensatory responses that upregulate APOL6 expression to mitigate the resulting functional impairment. Third, post-transcriptional regulation: SIRT4 may be involved in the stability regulation of APOL6 mRNA, and SIRT4 may bind to APOL6 mRNA, making APOL6 more prone to degradation. When SIRT4 is knocked out, the stability of APOL6 mRNA increases, which leads to an increase in the amount of APOL6 protein produced by translation.

This study still has several limitations. Although it is the first to discover the SIRT4-APOL6 pathway, the SIRT4-PC pathway, or possibly the SIRT4-APOL6-PC pathway, the precise molecular mechanisms underlying these pathways require further investigation. This study used a combination of in vivo and in vitro models for validation and conducted integrated multi-omics analyses to construct a comprehensive “metabolism-gene-function” trinity mechanism through non-targeted metabolomics (ATP abnormalities, PC abnormal accumulation), transcriptomics (upregulation of APOL6). This study first revealed that SIRT4 protects the optic nerve through the “APOL6-lipid metabolism axis” and the “mitochondrial dynamics axis” in a coordinated manner, and redefined the role of astrocytes, discovering that astrocytes regulate lipid secretion through the SIRT4-APOL6 pathway (Fig. 7), transforming from “passive support cells” to “active pathological drivers”, providing a new perspective for neurodegenerative diseases and a new noninvasive treatment strategy for optic nerve diseases such as glaucoma. Therefore further research on astrocyte lipid metabolism will better understand how apolipoproteins participate in glaucoma neurodegeneration and whether they can be used as biomarkers for glaucoma.
